Thank you for reaching out. We understand how frustrating it is to see a fee on a small coffee purchase, especially if you don't recall agreeing to overdraft coverage.

Under Regulation E, a bank generally may not charge a fee for paying an ATM or one-time debit card transaction under its overdraft service unless it has first given you a separate written (or, if you agree, electronic) notice describing the service, given you a reasonable opportunity to opt in, obtained your affirmative consent, and sent you written or electronic confirmation of that consent that includes your right to revoke it [R-1005.17#1]. For accounts opened on or after July 1, 2010, that consent must be obtained before any such fee is charged [R-1005.17#2]. The rule's definition of overdraft service excludes certain arrangements, such as a Regulation Z line of credit or an automatic transfer from another account of yours [R-1005.17#1]. If an account is joint, consent from any one joint holder counts as consent for the account [R-1005.17#3].

You may opt in at any time, and you may revoke consent at any time. The bank must implement a revocation as soon as reasonably practicable [R-1005.17#3].

Next steps: our team will review your account records, including whether and how consent was recorded and how this fee was classified. We will then respond to you with our findings. This is general information, not a decision on your case.

Thank you for contacting us, and we're sorry you were charged again after cancelling your gym membership and asking your bank to stop the payment. We understand how frustrating that is.

Under Regulation E, a consumer may stop payment of a preauthorized electronic fund transfer from their account by notifying the financial institution orally or in writing at least three business days before the scheduled date of the transfer [R-1005.10#1]. A financial institution may require written confirmation of an oral stop-payment order within 14 days of the oral notice [R-1005.10#1]. If it requires this, it must tell the consumer about the requirement and give the address for sending the confirmation when the consumer gives the oral notice [R-1005.10#1]. An oral stop-payment order ceases to be binding after 14 days if the consumer does not provide the required written confirmation [R-1005.10#1].

Next steps: our team will review the details of your case. That includes when you called, how far ahead of the scheduled charge it was, and whether written confirmation was requested. We will explain the outcome of that review to you. If you have notes of your call, a cancellation confirmation from the gym, or your statement showing the charge, please send them to us.

The sources available to us do not cover the bank's dispute timelines or what remedies may be available, so we cannot describe those here.

I'm sorry your birthday gift was reduced and then reported as expired. Here is general information on the rules; the team will review your card's details.

Under Regulation E, a store gift card is a card issued on a prepaid basis to a consumer in a specified amount, in exchange for payment, and redeemable at a single merchant or affiliated group of merchants [R-1005.20#1]. For covered cards, no one may impose a dormancy, inactivity, or service fee unless there has been no activity in the one-year period ending on the date the fee is imposed [R-1005.20#3]. The fee's amount, how often it may be charged, and that it may be assessed for inactivity must also be clearly and conspicuously stated on the card, and no more than one such fee may be imposed in a calendar month [R-1005.20#3].

On expiration, a card may be sold with an expiration date only if the underlying funds last at least five years from issuance or the date funds were last loaded, or until the card's expiration date if later, and required disclosures are given [R-1005.20#3]. Some cards produced before April 1, 2010 have temporary compliance rules [R-1005.20#4].

Next steps: the team will review the card, its disclosures, the dates and the fees charged. It may help to gather the card, packaging, receipt, and any fee notices. I can't say what the outcome will be.

We're sorry for the frustration of being charged a late fee and interest after paying online on the due date. Under Regulation Z, a card issuer generally must credit a payment to your account as of the date it is received, unless a delay in crediting does not result in a finance or other charge, or unless the issuer's permitted payment requirements apply [R-1026.10#1]. Issuers may set reasonable cut-off times for electronic payments, but those cut-off times may be no earlier than 5 p.m. on the due date [R-1026.10#1]. If an issuer promotes a payment method, payments made that way are treated as conforming and are credited as of the date of receipt, except when a delay does not result in a finance or other charge [R-1026.10#1]. If an issuer fails to credit a payment as required in time to avoid finance or other charges, it must adjust the account so those charges are credited during the next billing cycle [R-1026.10#2]. Our team will review the details, including when your payment was received, the payment method and the issuer's stated requirements, to determine how these rules apply to your account. Please send us your payment confirmation showing the date and time, and your statement showing the late fee and interest. We will explain our findings once the review is complete. We cannot promise a particular outcome now. The sources we reviewed do not cover the issuer's specific cut-off time or fee limits.

Thank you for writing to us. We understand it is frustrating when you pay well above the minimum and the balance carrying the 26% APR barely moves. Under Regulation Z, when a consumer pays more than the required minimum on a covered credit card account, the issuer must apply the excess first to the balance with the highest APR. Any remainder goes to the other balances in descending order of APR [R-1026.53#1]. There are special rules. For a balance under a deferred interest or similar program, where interest is not owed if the balance is paid in full before a set period ends, the rule gives two alternatives. Under the first, the excess follows the general rule, except in the two billing cycles right before the period expires, when it goes first to the deferred interest balance [R-1026.53#1]. Under the second, the issuer may at its option allocate the excess as the consumer requests [R-1026.53#1]. The issuer may also, at its option, apply excess to a secured balance if the consumer requests it [R-1026.53#1]. Our team will review your account, including how each balance is classified and how your payments were applied, and will tell you what we find. The sources available to us do not say whether your 0% balance falls under any exception, and they do not set response deadlines or remedies. Please keep your statements showing the payments and balances.

I'm sorry you are still waiting on a refund a month after asking for it in writing, especially after closing the account. Here is how the rules work in general. Under Regulation Z, when a credit balance of more than $1 is created on a credit account, the creditor must credit that amount to the account [R-1026.11#1]. It must also refund any remaining part of the balance within seven business days of receiving the consumer's written request [R-1026.11#1]. Separately, the creditor must make a good faith effort to refund any credit balance that stays on the account for more than six months by cash, check, money order, or credit to a deposit account. No further action is required if the consumer's current location is not known and cannot be traced through the last known address or telephone number [R-1026.11#1]. For merchandise returns, the rules say a merchant that accepts a return must send a credit statement to the card issuer within 7 business days, and the card issuer must then credit the account within 3 business days of receiving it [R-1026.12#3]. Our team will review the details of your account, including your return, the date your written request was received, and the current balance, to understand what happened and what steps apply. We cannot promise a particular outcome, but we will review the facts and tell you what we find. We're sorry your new laptop stopped working after a week and the store won't repair or refund it. That is frustrating, and yes, your card issuer may be able to help. Under federal rules, when a merchant that accepted your credit card fails to resolve a dispute about property or services you bought, you may assert against the card issuer claims (other than tort claims) and defenses arising from the transaction. You may also withhold payment up to the credit outstanding for that purchase and related finance or other charges [R-1026.12#2]. If you withhold that amount, the issuer may not report it as delinquent until the dispute is settled or judgment is rendered [R-1026.12#2]. These rights have conditions. You must have made a good faith attempt to resolve the dispute with the merchant. The purchase must also exceed $50, and it must have occurred in the same state as your current designated address or within 100 miles of it [R-1026.12#2]. Separate billing error procedures apply only to specific listed types of billing errors, such as property not accepted or not delivered as agreed, so they may not cover a defective item [R-1026.13#1]. Our team will review the details of your purchase and your efforts to resolve this with the store, and will tell you what we need from you next. We cannot promise a particular outcome.

These rights apply only if you made a good faith attempt to resolve the dispute with the merchant, and if the amount of credit extended exceeds $50 and the transaction occurred in the same state as your current designated address or within 100 miles of it [R-1026.12#2]. Certain exclusions to the location and amount limits exist, for example where the merchant is the card issuer or is controlled by it [R-1026.12#2]. Thank you for reaching out, and we're sorry that repeated calls to your workplace are causing you stress. Here is general information about the rules that apply. Under Regulation F, a debt collector must not communicate or attempt to communicate with a consumer about a debt at the consumer's place of employment if the collector knows or has reason to know that the consumer's employer prohibits the consumer from receiving such communication [R-1006.6#1]. Collectors also must not contact a consumer at a place the collector knows or should know is inconvenient to the consumer [R-1006.6#1]. These prohibitions have exceptions: they do not apply if the consumer gave prior consent directly to the collector during a communication that did not itself violate these rules, or if a court of competent jurisdiction expressly permitted the contact [R-1006.6#1]. Separately, if a consumer notifies a collector in writing that the consumer wants it to cease further communication, the collector generally must not communicate further about that debt, subject to exceptions stated in the regulation [R-1006.6#1]. A collector also must not use a medium of communication the person has asked it not to use [R-1006.14#2]. Next steps: our team will review the details of your complaint, including the calls you describe and what the collector was told. We cannot say now what the outcome will be. It may help to keep a record of the dates and times of the calls. The sources we reviewed do not specify how a consumer must tell a collector about an employer's call restrictions, so we cannot address that detail here.

Under Regulation F, a debt collector must not communicate or attempt to communicate with a consumer about a debt at the consumer's place of employment if the collector knows or has reason to know that the employer prohibits the consumer from receiving such communication [R-1006.6#1]. There are exceptions: this does not apply if the consumer gave prior consent directly to the collector during a communication that did not itself violate these rules, or if a court has given express permission [R-1006.6#1]. The rule also sets call-frequency presumptions: a collector is presumed to violate the rule if it exceeds seven calls within seven consecutive days to a person about a particular debt, or calls within seven days after a telephone conversation about that debt, subject to certain exclusions [R-1006.14#1]. We're sorry you received a voicemail like this; a threat of arrest and a demand for same-day payment can be frightening. Under Regulation F, a debt collector must not engage in conduct whose natural consequence is to harass, oppress, or abuse any person in connection with collecting a debt [R-1006.14#1]. A collector also must not use or threaten to use violence or other criminal means to harm a person's physical person, reputation, or property [R-1006.14#1]. Collectors must not use unfair or unconscionable means to collect a debt, and must not collect any amount unless it is expressly authorized by the agreement creating the debt or permitted by law [R-1006.22#1]. Regulation F also sets call-frequency rules. A collector is presumed to violate the harassment rule if it calls about a particular debt more than seven times within seven consecutive days, or within seven consecutive days after a telephone conversation about that debt [R-1006.14#1]. Some calls do not count toward those limits, such as calls not connected to the dialed number, or calls placed with consent given directly to the collector and only within seven consecutive days after receiving that consent [R-1006.14#1]. Our team will review the details of your situation, including the voicemail. It would help to keep the voicemail, note the date and time of each call, and save any letters. The sources we reviewed do not address how to dispute a debt, or give a timeframe for our review, so we cannot say how long it will take or what the outcome will be.

I'm sorry you received this voicemail. A message threatening arrest and demanding immediate payment is stressful, and we take it seriously. Under Regulation F, a debt collector must not use any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with collecting a debt [R-1006.18#1]. A collector also must not represent or imply that nonpayment will result in arrest or imprisonment unless that action is lawful and the collector or creditor intends to take it [R-1006.18#1]. More generally, a collector must not threaten any action that cannot legally be taken or that is not intended to be taken [R-1006.18#1]. Collectors also must not falsely represent the character, amount, or legal status of a debt [R-1006.18#1]. Separately, a collector must not engage in conduct whose natural consequence is to harass, oppress, or abuse a person, and must not use or threaten to use criminal means to harm a person's physical person, reputation, or property [R-1006.14#1]. Our team will review the voicemail and the surrounding details to assess how these rules apply. We will review the information, and the evidence we have does not tell us how any particular review will end. Before charging an overdraft fee on an ATM withdrawal, a bank must get the consumer's affirmative opt-in to its overdraft service for ATM and one-time debit card transactions. Regulation E bars the fee unless the institution does all of the following [R-1005.17#1]:

1. Gives a written notice (or electronic, if the consumer agrees), segregated from other information, describing the overdraft service [R-1005.17#1].
2. Provides a reasonable opportunity to opt in [R-1005.17#1].
3. Obtains the consumer's affirmative consent [R-1005.17#1].
4. Confirms the consent in writing (or electronically, if the consumer agrees), including a statement of the right to revoke [R-1005.17#1].

Notice content: The notice must be substantially similar to Model Form A-9. It must describe the service, state the fee amounts (the maximum fee if the amount varies), state the maximum number of fees per day or that there is no limit, explain the opt-in right and how to consent, and mention any Regulation Z credit line or linked-account transfer alternative [R-1005.17#2].

Timing: For accounts opened on or after July 1, 2010, the bank must comply and obtain consent before assessing any such fee [R-1005.17#2]. For earlier accounts, the same condition applied to fees on or after August 15, 2010 [R-1005.17#2].

Other limits: A bank cannot condition payment of other overdrafts (checks, ACH) on the consumer's consent, and must give non-consenting consumers the same account terms, conditions, and features [R-1005.17#1]. A debt collector is presumed to comply with the ban on repeated or continuous calls if it places calls to a particular person about a particular debt neither more than seven times within seven consecutive days, nor within seven consecutive days after having had a telephone conversation with the person about that debt [R-1006.14#1]. Calls exceeding either frequency are presumed to violate the rule, subject to the exclusions in paragraph (b)(3) [R-1006.14#1]. Those exclusions cover calls placed with the person's prior consent given directly to the collector (within seven consecutive days after the consent), calls not connected to the dialed number, and calls to certain persons described in § 1006.6(d)(1)(ii) through (vi) [R-1006.14#1]. Separately, the general rule bars calls made repeatedly or continuously with intent to annoy, abuse, or harass [R-1006.14#1]. Timing rules in § 1006.6(b) also say that, absent contrary knowledge, before 8:00 a.m. and after 9:00 p.m. local time is inconvenient [R-1006.6#1].
